indications.text: First identify and remove precipitating factors: hypoxia, ischemia, electrolytes. Then set the goal: terminate an ongoing arrhythmia or prevent arrhythmia (symptoms, frequency and reproducibility, structural damage).
indications.edu: Minimize risk: every antiarrhythmic may itself induce arrhythmias, so understand the mechanism before choosing. Ischemia changes the resting membrane potential, conduction velocity, intracellular calcium and repolarization rate, so the heart's electrophysiology is a moving target.
verify: termination of ongoing arrhythmia or prevention of arrhythmia

indications.text: Supraventricular tachycardia, ventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation prevention and prevention of premature ventricular contractions.
indications.edu: Class I as a whole works on both supraventricular and ventricular arrhythmias.
verify: Supraventricular tachycardia, ventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation prevention and PVC prevention

indications.text: Ventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation prevention, symptomatic ventricular beats.
indications.edu: Every class IB indication is ventricular.
verify: Ventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation prevention, symptomatic ventricular beats

indications.text: Life-threatening ventricular tachycardia or fibrillation; refractory supraventricular tachycardia.
indications.edu: Reserved for the serious or refractory cases.
verify: Life threatening ventricular tachycardia, or fibrillation, refractory supraventricular  tachycardia

indications.text: Supraventricular tachycardia, fibrillation.
indications.edu: Supraventricular arrhythmias are the main use.

indications.text: Refractory ventricular tachycardia, atrial fibrillation, flutter, supraventricular tachycardia.
indications.edu: Like class I, class III covers both supraventricular and ventricular arrhythmias.
verify: Class III - Refractory ventricular tachycardia, atrial fibrillation, flutter, supraventricular tachycardia

indications.drug:
Class IV and the miscellaneous agents
verapamil, diltiazem; adenosine, digoxin
indications.text: Supraventricular tachycardia (both).
indications.edu: No ventricular indication is listed for class IV or the miscellaneous agents.

indications.drug:
Quinidine
class IA; a D-isomer of quinine
indications.text: Maintain rhythm with atrial flutter or fibrillation; control ventricular tachycardia; conversion of atrial flutter and fibrillation (very limited use; the same slide lists anticoagulants and digitalis under conversion).
indications.edu: Diarrhea and nausea are very common (30 to 50 percent); report ringing in the ears, dizziness or blurred vision (cinchonism).
verify: Maintain rhythm with atrial flutter or fibrillation
Conversion of Atrial Flutter and Fibrillation (very limited use)

indications.drug:
Procainamide
class IA; an amide derivative of procaine
indications.text: The class IA uses. Short duration of action (3 to 4 hours), so a slow-release preparation is used. Intravenous: better tolerated than quinidine. Oral: poorly tolerated long term.
indications.edu: A lupus-like syndrome is common (25 to 50 percent), more often in slow acetylators: report new symptoms that could be part of it.
verify: Lupus like syndrome (25-50%, more often in slow acetylators)
Short duration of action (3 - 4 hours) Slow release preparation

indications.text: Ventricular tachycardia; supraventricular arrhythmias (flutter, fibrillation).
indications.edu: Stronger anticholinergic actions than quinidine and a negative inotropic effect: contraindicated in glaucoma and heart block, and it can bring on heart failure.

indications.text: Ventricular tachycardia and premature beats; ventricular fibrillation; acute myocardial infarction; Wolff-Parkinson-White is also listed. Current guidelines differ: lidocaine is not a recommended treatment for Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome.
indications.edu: Given intravenously only (extensive first-pass metabolism). Not effective against atrial arrhythmias. Works best on sodium channels in ischemic tissue.

verify: Most effective on Na channels in ischemic tissue

indications.text: Life-threatening sustained ventricular arrhythmias; supraventricular arrhythmias; prevents premature ventricular contractions.
indications.edu: Use only in patients without significant structural damage to the heart (it increases mortality after a myocardial infarction). Long half-life (14 hours); oral or intravenous.
verify: Use only in patients without significant structural damage to heart
Long half- life (14 hours), Oral, IV

indications.drug:
Propafenone
class IC with beta-blocking activity
indications.text: The class IC uses; same mechanism as flecainide plus beta-blocking activity.
indications.edu: The beta-blocking activity brings bronchospasm, bradycardia and worsening heart failure; it is also proarrhythmic.

indications.drug:
Propranolol
class II; nonselective beta blocker
indications.text: Supraventricular arrhythmias; ventricular ectopic beats; myocardial infarction.
indications.edu: Nonselective, so bronchospasm is a risk: report wheeze or breathlessness. It can also worsen heart failure and cause heart block.

indications.drug:
Metoprolol, acebutolol, esmolol
class II; beta-1 selective
indications.text: Similar to propranolol, with less bronchospasm (beta-1 selective). Esmolol is the intravenous, short-acting beta blocker.
indications.edu: Can still cause heart failure, and sedation and fatigue.

indications.drug:
Amiodarone
class III; an analog of thyroid hormone
indications.text: Recurrent ventricular tachycardia or fibrillation resistant to other drugs; maintain normal rate in atrial fibrillation. Intravenous: terminates acute ventricular tachycardia or fibrillation, replacing lidocaine in myocardial infarction. Current guidelines differ: resuscitation guidance lists amiodarone or lidocaine as options for shock-refractory ventricular fibrillation or pulseless ventricular tachycardia.
indications.edu: Oral and intravenous. Half-life about 40 days (26 to 107): slow onset, slow elimination, so loading doses may be needed. Report cough or breathlessness, a blue-gray skin color or easy sunburn, and vision changes.
verify: Recurrent ventricular tachycardia or fibrillation resistant to other drugs
maintain normal rate in atrial fibrillation
terminate acute ventricular tachycardia or fibrillation replacing lidocaine in MI

indications.drug:
Dofetilide
class III; potent pure potassium channel blocker
indications.text: Normal rhythm in atrial fibrillation. Limited availability to those with special training.
indications.edu: Mainly eliminated unchanged by the kidneys. Torsades de pointes (1 to 3 percent) and marked QT prolongation are its adverse effects.
verify: Limited availability to those with special training

indications.drug:
Sotalol
class III with beta-blocking activity
indications.text: Atrial flutter and fibrillation; ventricular tachyarrhythmia.
indications.edu: Beta-blocking activity as well as potassium channel block: torsades de pointes and bronchospasm are its adverse effects.
verify: Indications: atrial flutter and fibrillation, ventricular tachyarrhythmia

indications.drug:
Verapamil, diltiazem
class IV; calcium channel blockers
indications.text: Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia; atrial fibrillation.
indications.edu: Hypotension and edema are expected; hepatic metabolism, so caution in liver damage. Avoid in ventricular arrhythmias, sick sinus syndrome and depressed cardiac function.
verify: Hepatic metabolism, caution in liver damage
Avoid in ventricular arrhythmias, sick sinus syndrome, depressed cardiac function

indications.text: Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia; Wolff-Parkinson-White is also listed. Current guidelines differ: adenosine can end the reentrant tachycardia of Wolff-Parkinson-White but is avoided when the syndrome presents as pre-excited atrial fibrillation.
indications.edu: Warn the patient: it may stop the heart for 2 to 3 seconds, and flushing, shortness of breath and burning in the chest can occur; its half-life is only about 10 seconds.

indications.text: Slow the ventricular rate; induce heart block in atrial flutter and fibrillation.
indications.edu: Report nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, loss of appetite, confusion or visual disturbances. Combining it with calcium channel blockers or beta blockers is to be avoided.

indications.text: Torsades de pointes, given intravenously: the only indication on its slide.
indications.edu: Watch for bradycardia, flushing, headache and, the dangerous one, respiratory paralysis.

sideeffects.text: All antiarrhythmics may induce arrhythmias.
sideeffects.monitor: Understand the mechanism and weigh the goal (termination or prevention) against the risk; remove precipitating factors first.

sideeffects.monitor: The most common reason the drug is poorly tolerated.

Added background (not on the slides): quinidine carries a Food and Drug Administration (FDA) boxed warning for increased mortality when it is used for arrhythmias that are not life-threatening.

charts.title: Antiarrhythmic Drugs Compared by Class
charts.sub: Classes I to IV and the three miscellaneous agents side by side: what each blocks, what it does to the action potential (read off the slide pictures), what it does to conduction, what it is for, what it causes and what to avoid.
charts.notes: Read the indications column for the trend. Class I and class III work on both supraventricular and ventricular arrhythmias; class II, class IV and the miscellaneous agents are listed for supraventricular arrhythmias (propranolol's slide adds ventricular ectopic beats, and verapamil and diltiazem are to be avoided in ventricular arrhythmias). Read the action potential column for the mechanism: class IA and IC slow phase 0 (IC the most), class IB shortens the action potential and works mainly in ischemic tissue, class III lengthens repolarization, and class II and IV flatten phase 4 in the pacemaker cells of the sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodes. Torsades de pointes belongs to the drugs that lengthen repolarization (class IA, dofetilide, sotalol) and is treated with magnesium sulfate. Doses are not tested and are left out.
